newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium physical premiums strong, business thin.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium physical premiums strong, business thin.

text.p: Aluminium physical premiums in Europe remain at robust levels, but activity is thin due to heated futures prices and holidays, traders said.
"Europe continues to be very boring. The LME (price) is too high for most of Europe," one said.
Russian A7E metal, which is deliverable on the London Metal Exchange (LME), was quoted at around $42/$52 per tonne over LME cash, cif Rotterdam, compared to $30/$40 about a month ago.
"The A7E has to be at those levels to attract metal into Rotterdam," another trader said.
Duty unpaid Western metal in Rotterdam was steady at a $50/$60 premium and duty paid was at $130/$140.
In Europe there has been limited forward interest, after most consumers trimmed their operations to run with a minimum of stocks.
Offtake in Japan and the United States is strong, with much of the metal leaving LME warehouses going to the U.S., traders said.
LME inventories fell by another 3,175 tonnes on Wednesday, bringing to 8,925 tonnes the total erosion since Monday. Last week stocks declined by 14,275 tonnes.
Stocks are expected to keep falling in the near term and premiums are expected to stay firm through June, one trader said.
The May Day and Ascension Day holidays in continental Europe and the two Bank holidays in Britain have put a damper on activity.
In the zinc market, high futures prices are inhibiting business, traders said.
"Since the LME price went over $1,300, our business has dried up. They are only taking bits and pieces," one said.
"Most of our customers are convinced that prices are going to dip," he added.
Three months LME prices on Wednesday afternoon rechallenged their 1997 high of $1,340 hit on Monday.
Physical premiums were steady at $25/$30 over LME cash for special high grade metal in Rotterdam and were a touch higher at flat to a $10 premium for CIS metal in Rotterdam, traders said.
